projects.title: AERONEX
projects.sub: Open-source ground station for ArduCopter drones
projects.kind: Software & AI · Robotics · Ground control station
projects.desc: AERONEX is a free, open-source ground station for ArduCopter drones that I designed and built, shipped as a Windows app. It takes one aircraft through its whole life in a single place: design the frame, import its CAD model as a digital twin, install firmware, calibrate and tune, rehearse in a physics simulator, plan and fly the mission, then read the flight log. It grew out of AVION, where setting up and flying our drone meant juggling several tools written for experts. AERONEX is written for the student holding their first Pixhawk: every page says in plain words what it does, what it does not, and what to do next.

video.caption: The AERONEX film: 44 seconds from design to flight

images.caption: AERONEX overview: the aircraft's 3D model with its live instruments, here on the built-in virtual aircraft
Frame Studio: five questions about the parts you own become a frame with its weight, balance and hover throttle worked out
Digital Twin: the real CAD assembly, imported and oriented, ready to fly on screen
Firmware: the right ArduCopter build is chosen for the board and every byte is checked after writing
Mission Planning: a five-waypoint route with its length, flight-time prediction and ground clearance
Flight Simulator: a 450-class quadcopter in GUIDED mode, with wind and fault injection
Flight Logs: a report that says what went wrong in the flight and what to do about it
Log replay: the recorded flight played back in 3D beside its instruments

chapters.title: Why I built it
chapters.text: On AVION, our disaster-relief drone, the ground side was a patchwork: one program to flash firmware, another to calibrate, a third to plan the mission, and our own page for the live view. Each assumed you already knew ArduPilot. AERONEX puts the whole job in one app, in the order you would do it — design, set up, fly, review — and explains each step as it goes. It is free, open source under Apache 2.0, and needs no account.

chapters.title: Design the aircraft
chapters.text: Frame Studio starts from the parts you own. Answer five questions about propellers, motors, battery and material, and it works out the geometry, all-up weight, thrust-to-weight ratio and hover throttle, then hands over the files to cut or print (DXF, SVG, PDF, STL) with a parts list. No CAD is needed to get a frame that balances.

chapters.title: A digital twin of the real airframe
chapters.text: If the aircraft already exists in CAD, AERONEX imports the assembly directly — STEP, GLB, OBJ or STL — read in the browser and never uploaded. You set which way is forward and up once, and the same model then appears everywhere: on the overview, in the simulator and in log replay.

chapters.title: Set up without guesswork
chapters.text: The firmware page picks the correct stable ArduCopter build from 316 board definitions generated from ArduPilot's own hardware files, writes it, and verifies it. Sensor, radio, ESC and flight-mode calibration, motor test, PID tuning and servo outputs follow, and every parameter carries ArduPilot's own description, units and range. A preflight check then gives a go or no-go verdict that follows ArduCopter's pre-arm checks.

chapters.title: Rehearse before the props spin
chapters.text: The built-in virtual aircraft is a six-degree-of-freedom physics model stepped at 400 Hz that speaks real MAVLink, so every page of the app works against it exactly as it would against a flight controller. You can fly it from the keyboard, add wind, and inject faults to see how the aircraft and the app respond. Simulated data is always labelled as simulated.

chapters.title: Plan the mission
chapters.text: Missions are drawn on a real map over measured ground heights, with a geofence, payload delivery and a flight-time prediction. Uploads are read back from the aircraft and compared before the app calls them sent. Against ArduCopter itself in simulation, flown waypoints landed within 1.5 m of the plan, and a predicted 98-second flight took 104 seconds.

chapters.title: Review the flight
chapters.text: Flight Logs opens ArduPilot .bin and .tlog files, checks them for vibration, power and GPS problems, and says what it found and what to do. Any field can be charted, and the flight can be replayed in 3D. Drone Doctor does the same for a connected aircraft: a health scan that names the fault and the fix.

chapters.title: Built to be trusted
chapters.text: A ground station sends commands to a real aircraft, so safety is designed in. Commands go only to ArduCopter and wait for the aircraft to confirm each one; motor tests need a props-off confirmation; a lost link hands over to the aircraft's own failsafe. The MAVLink parser was written from scratch and validates the checksum of every frame. More than 780 unit tests cover the code, and 39 flight tests run against ArduPilot's own simulator on ArduCopter 4.6 and 4.7. AERONEX has been connected to a physical Pixhawk 2.4.8, and release 0.3.7 is available to download.

projects.title: AVION
projects.desc: An autonomous quadcopter that delivers medikits and food parcels to people cut off by floods and landslides. A Raspberry Pi 4 flies the mission through a Pixhawk autopilot, finds colour-marked drop zones with an Intel RealSense D455 depth camera and releases the parcel with a servo hook. A browser ground station with a live 3D digital twin keeps an operator in command of every drop. In-house carbon-fibre and 3D-printed airframe; presented at the ROBOFEST Gujarat 6.0 Hackathon.

images.caption: AVION on the test field: carbon-fibre frame with 3D-printed joints
AVION and its ground station at the ROBOFEST Gujarat 6.0 Hackathon
Ground station: operator-checked parcel reload with live 3D digital twin
Browser-based digital simulator of the relief mission
In-house printable parts: frame joints, payload hook and avionics mounts

chapters.title: The problem
chapters.text: After a flood or a landslide, the people who need help most are the ones a road can no longer reach. AVION is a quadcopter that carries a medikit or a food parcel to a marked drop zone, finds the zone itself and releases the parcel — while an operator on the ground stays in command of every drop.

chapters.title: Airframe
chapters.text: The frame is carbon-fibre tube joined by parts we printed in-house: frame joints, the avionics mounts and the payload hook. Printing our own parts meant a broken joint on the field was a reprint away, not a reorder.

chapters.title: Flight stack
chapters.text: A Pixhawk 2.4.8 running ArduPilot holds the aircraft. A Raspberry Pi 4 sits beside it as the companion computer and flies the mission over MAVLink with DroneKit — take-off, waypoints, search, drop and return.

chapters.title: Perception and the drop
chapters.text: An Intel RealSense D455 gives the Pi depth and colour. OpenCV finds the colour-marked drop zone, the Pi centres the aircraft over it and descends, and a servo hook lets the parcel go.

chapters.title: Ground station
chapters.text: A browser ground station — Flask and Socket.IO behind it, a Three.js digital twin in front — shows the operator the aircraft's attitude and position live, walks them through an operator-checked parcel reload, and runs the whole mission in a browser-based simulator before anything flies.

chapters.title: Rehearsal
chapters.text: Every mission was flown in the simulator first: the same ground station, the same waypoints, a virtual aircraft. It caught the mistakes that would have cost an airframe.

chapters.title: Result
chapters.text: AVION reached the finals of ROBOFEST Gujarat 6.0, India's biggest robotics hackathon, organised by GUJCOST at RAC Bhavnagar. The ground station has since grown into AERONEX, a standalone station for ArduPilot aircraft.

projects.title: TerraAvis
projects.desc: An AI-enabled hybrid rescue robot with a dual-mode mobility system combining aerial navigation and tracked ground movement. Integrated thermal imaging, FPV surveillance, real-time object detection and autonomous control for search-and-rescue and disaster-response scenarios.

projects.title: 4-Bit Microprocessor
projects.sub: Built from discrete logic on breadboards
projects.desc: A fully functional 4-bit microprocessor built entirely from discrete 74-series logic ICs on breadboards. Complete datapath including ALU, registers, instruction register, program counter and shared bus, with a hardwired control unit and a custom instruction set supporting arithmetic, logical, load, store and conditional jump operations.

images.caption: The working processor, wired on breadboards from 74-series logic ICs
Datapath simulation: registers, adder–subtractor and bus buffers

projects.title: Friendly AI Chatbot
projects.desc: A standalone embedded AI device built around an ESP32 with real-time voice input, amplified audio output and an OLED display for feedback. Includes a custom-designed PCB and 3D-printed enclosure, with Python driving the conversational logic.

images.caption: 3D-printed enclosure with speaker grille and OLED window

Enclosure prepared for printing in Bambu Studio

projects.title: Dual-Axis CNC Plotter
projects.sub: Motion control from G-code to paper
projects.desc: A 2-axis CNC plotter using Arduino, stepper motors and a custom mechanical frame to translate digital designs into precise physical drawings. Implemented G-code interpretation and motion-control firmware for accurate pen positioning, combining embedded systems with mechanical design.

images.caption: Fusion 360 model of the dual-axis frame and stepper drives

projects.title: DoseGuard
projects.kind: Decision systems · Nuclear science · Data design
projects.desc: A standards-grounded decision engine for gamma irradiation, built on 30+ IAEA research papers and cross-referenced against each destination country's own regulatory limits (e.g. FDA 21 CFR 179.26). Generates a downloadable, accurate prescription report with tailored recommendations for your exact product and facility. Built for HackAtom Summer University 2026.

images.caption: From product to validated dose: the DoseGuard console
A compliant prescription, with the dose physics behind it
The deliverable: a one-click, auditable PDF prescription report
